What did the longer letters say about RPM documentation burden versus payment?

comments.text: The step I'd most want audited is the chart and table transcription. Quoted text gets checked by whoever quotes it, but a number lifted from a scanned bar chart rarely gets checked by anyone. When we had a model read photographed handwritten lists, we settled on making it flag every value it was unsure of instead of returning a clean guess. A per-cell confidence column in those SQLite tables would tell readers which numbers to recheck.

comments.text:
Matthew Holt Yours would have brought the tally above 1/10k ;) Only four comments say fee for service should be scrapped in favour of a subscription-style payment: a flat, recurring sum per patient.

- A health-plan analyst says per-visit pay forces doctors to carry huge patient lists to stay profitable. He argues "Primary Care needs to no longer be fee based" and points to capitated and direct-primary-care models instead. (https://joshuamandel.com/regulations.gov-comment-browser/CMS-2026-2377/#/comments/CMS-2026-2377-14244)

- An anonymous paediatrician wants primary care "paid more like a gym membership": about $200–250 per child per month for access to a paediatrician, with specialists funded by a separate payment of the same kind. (CMS-2026-2377-26009)

- Andrew Schutzbank, an internist and early Iora Health leader, says fee-for-service pays for visits when patients need continuity. The plan he proposes ends: "Gradually fade out fee-for-service revenue." (CMS-2026-2377-30763)

comments.text:
There’s an interesting implication here for the organizations submitting these comments too.

When tens of thousands of submissions can be analyzed this quickly, volume becomes much easier to separate from substance. That could change the value of the comment itself. A hundred variations of the same argument may still demonstrate constituency, but a well-supported submission with distinctive evidence or operational insight becomes much easier to find in a dataset this large.

The technology isn’t just making the public record easier to analyze. It may eventually change how organizations think about contributing to it in the first place.
